title: Episode 330: Queen Victoria (Part 2): The Widow of Windsor, Disraeli, Gladstone, Empress of India, and the Diamond Jubilee
description:
The monumental, legendary second half of Queen Victoria's historic reign. Following the tragic death of Prince Albert in 1861, Victoria withdrew into four decades of permanent mourning black, retreating from London to Windsor, Balmoral, and Osborne as the 'Widow of Windsor'. Re-emerging onto the national stage through her extraordinary, affectionate partnership with Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli, Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. Navigating bitter political clashes with William Gladstone and the expansion of the British Empire across Africa and Asia, Victoria celebrated her Golden and Diamond Jubilees as the living symbol of an empire upon which the sun never set. Discover the Matriarch of Empire.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series concludes our two-part saga of Queen Victoria: chronicling the four decades of mourning, the imperial triumph in India, and the breathtaking Diamond Jubilee of the world's most powerful matriarch: Queen Victoria. Here is George with part two: the Widow of Windsor.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE HERMIT OF WINDSOR: GRIEF AND SECLUSION: 1861 TO 1868
Following Albert's death in December 1861, Victoria surrendered completely to a culture of monumental, obsessive mourning. She commanded that Albert's private dressing room at Windsor be kept exactly as he left it: fresh hot water was placed in his shaving mug each morning, clean clothes laid upon his bed, and his chamber pots emptied as if he were still alive. For the rest of her life—thirty-nine long years—Victoria dressed exclusively in mourning black crepe, white widow's cap, and jet jewelry. She retreated from London, dividing her year between Windsor Castle, Osborne House, and her beloved Scottish estate of Balmoral. Her absolute refusal to open Parliament, inspect troops, or appear in public provoked widespread republican discontent: in 1864, a sarcastic notice was pinned to the gates of Buckingham Palace: 'These commanding premises to be let or sold, in consequence of the late occupant's retiring from business.' Satirists mocked her as 'Mrs. Brown', referencing her close, controversial friendship with her rugged, kilted Scottish servant, John Brown, who spoke to the sovereign with blunt Highland familiarity and helped her survive her deepest depression. For nearly a decade following Albert's passing, Queen Victoria became virtually invisible to her subjects, refusing to open Parliament, review troops, or attend public state ceremonies. Republican sentiment began to fester across Britain: pamphlets appeared on the gates of Buckingham Palace mocking 'These commanding premises to be let or sold, in consequence of the late occupant's retirement from business'. In her secluded highland retreat at Balmoral Castle, Victoria found solace only in the rugged company of John Brown, her personal gillie. Brown's gruff, unvarnished honesty and fierce devotion provided the grieving queen with a protective buffer against court protocol and intrusive politicians, though scandalous rumors of their intimacy swirled through London society, earning the reclusive monarch the satirical nickname 'Mrs. Brown'.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE FLATTERER AND THE PREACHER: DISRAELI AND GLADSTONE
Victoria's return to public political engagement was orchestrated by her contrasting relationships with the two titan Prime Ministers of the late Victorian era: Benjamin Disraeli and William Ewart Gladstone. Disraeli, the flamboyant, Jewish-born Tory romantic, shamelessly flattered the Queen, treating her with poetic gallantry, famously observing: 'Everyone likes flattery; and when it comes to royalty, you should lay it on with a trowel.' Victoria was captivated, calling Disraeli 'dear Mr. Disraeli' and exchanging bouquets of primroses. By contrast, she detested the austere, high-minded Liberal William Gladstone, complaining bitterly: 'He speaks to me as if I were a public meeting!' When Disraeli purchased four million pounds of Suez Canal shares in 1875 from the Khedive of Egypt, securing Britain's maritime highway to India, he presented the triumph to Victoria as a personal gift: 'It is just settled; you have it, Madam!' The contrast between Disraeli and Gladstone came to define the great parliamentary dramas of the high Victorian era. Gladstone was an earnest, moralizing intellectual who approached politics as a religious crusade, delivering thunderous four-hour speeches on Bulgarian atrocities and Irish Home Rule that exhausted and irritated the Queen. Victoria famously complained: 'He speaks to me as if I were a public meeting!' Disraeli, by contrast, was a romantic novelist and master psychologist who understood how to reignite Victoria's pride in her sovereign destiny. He flattered her lavishly, confiding to a friend: 'Everyone likes flattery; and when you come to royalty, you should lay it on with a trowel!' Disraeli's daring purchase of a forty-four percent stake in the Suez Canal in 1875 secured Britain's imperial artery to India and enchanted the Queen completely.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: EMPRESS OF INDIA: THE IMPERIAL CROWN: 1876
Disraeli's supreme stroke of imperial flattery came in 1876 with the Royal Titles Act. Anxious that her eldest daughter Victoria, Crown Princess of Prussia, would outrank her when she became German Empress, Victoria pressured Disraeli to create an imperial title for the British Crown. On May 1, 1876, Queen Victoria was officially proclaimed Kaisar-i-Hind—Empress of India. The title captured Victoria's romantic imagination: she viewed the subcontinent with deep personal affection, learning to write Hindustani, surrounding herself with Indian servants led by Abdul Karim, the 'Munshi', who taught her Urdu and cooked authentic curries, and fiercely condemning racial prejudice among British colonial officers. Victoria became the living, mystical embodiment of the British Empire, uniting hundreds of millions of diverse subjects under her symbolic maternal protection across a territory covering a quarter of the globe. The proclamation of Queen Victoria as Kaiser-i-Hind—Empress of India—in 1877 transformed the psychological relationship between the British monarchy and the subcontinent. Though Victoria never physically set foot in India due to the grueling sea voyage, she developed an intense, affectionate fascination with Indian culture and languages. She learned to write in Hindustani and Urdu under the tutelage of her Indian attendant, Abdul Karim—known as the Munshi—who taught her Indian customs and prepared curry in the royal kitchen. Despite furious protests from aristocratic courtiers who viewed the Munshi with racial condescension, Victoria fiercely defended her Indian servant, insisting that all her Indian subjects be treated with dignity and equal respect under the imperial crown.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GOLDEN JUBILEE OF 1887: FIFTY YEARS OF GLORY
In June 1887, Great Britain and the Empire celebrated Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, marking fifty years upon the throne. London was transformed into an imperial carnival of bunting, triumphal arches, and gas illuminations. On June 21, fifty foreign kings and European princes, along with Indian maharajas in turbans encrusted with diamonds and emeralds, escorted the Queen in an open landau carriage through streets packed with millions of cheering citizens to Westminster Abbey. Victoria wore a black silk dress with panels of white lace and a white bonnet adorned with diamonds. At Westminster Abbey, sitting upon the ancient Coronation Chair, Victoria kissed her children and grandchildren, deeply moved by the thunderous affection of her people. The Golden Jubilee marked the complete rehabilitation of the monarchy: the lonely 'Widow of Windsor' had become the beloved, venerated grandmother of the British Empire. The Golden Jubilee of 1887 was an emotional turning point that brought Queen Victoria back into the adoring embrace of her people. Kings, princes, and tribal rulers from every corner of the earth marched behind the royal landau, accompanied by an escort of fifty imperial princes on horseback. As the Queen took her seat upon King Edward's ancient coronation chair in Westminster Abbey, the congregation broke into thunderous applause, moved to tears by the sight of the tiny, elderly matriarch who had guided the British nation through fifty years of unprecedented transformation. Victoria wrote in her diary that evening: 'No one ever, I believe, has met with such an ovation as was given to me, passing through those six miles of streets... The warmth and enthusiasm was indescribable.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DIAMOND JUBILEE: THE IMPERIAL ZENITH: JUNE 1897
Ten years later, in June 1897, came the supreme, unequaled spectacle of British imperial majesty: the Diamond Jubilee, celebrating sixty years of Victoria's reign. At seventy-eight, so crippled by arthritis that she could not mount the steps of St. Paul's Cathedral, the procession was designed so the service could be held outside on the cathedral steps with the Queen remaining in her open carriage. The procession through London was an astonishing military display of global power: fifty thousand soldiers from every corner of the earth marched behind the royal carriage—Canadian Mounties, Australian bush cavalry, New Zealand Maoris, Hong Kong police, Jamaican artillerymen, Indian lancers, and African Hausa riflemen. As the carriage paused before St. Paul's, the Archbishop of Canterbury led the crowd in the Te Deum, and Victoria wept behind her black parasol, whispering: 'How kind they are to me!' It was the absolute zenith of the British Empire, an unmatched moment of pride, prosperity, and global preeminence. The Diamond Jubilee of 1897 brought over fifty thousand imperial troops to London: Canadian Mounties in scarlet tunics, turbaned Sikhs from the Punjab, West Indian riflemen, Australian bushmen, and Maori soldiers from New Zealand marched side by side in an awe-inspiring display of global unity. Suffering from severe arthritis, Victoria remained seated in her carriage during the thanksgiving service on the steps of St. Paul's Cathedral, her eyes glistening with tears as a choir of five hundred voices sang the Te Deum. Before leaving Buckingham Palace that morning, she had pressed an electric button that transmitted a telegraphic message across underwater cables to every corner of her global empire: 'From my heart I thank my beloved people. May God bless them!' It was the zenith of an empire upon which the sun never set.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SHADOW OF THE BOER WAR: 1899 TO 1900
The sunset of Victoria's reign was darkened by the bitter, bloody ordeal of the Second Boer War in South Africa. When British forces suffered catastrophic defeats during 'Black Week' in December 1899 at Stormberg, Magersfontein, and Colenso, the eighty-year-old queen displayed the unyielding martial fortitude of her warrior ancestors. When the diplomat Arthur Balfour expressed anxiety over the reverses, Queen Victoria famously rebuked him with iron majesty: 'Please understand that there is no one depressed in this house; we are not interested in the possibilities of defeat; they do not exist.' She visited wounded soldiers at Netley Hospital, presented chocolate tins to troops in South Africa, and in April 1900 made a courageous three-week state visit to Dublin to thank the Irish regiments for their heroism, despite serious fears of republican assassination. The Boer War was a painful, bloody awakening for the late Victorian British Empire. During 'Black Week' in December 1899, British armies suffered catastrophic defeats at Stormberg, Magersfontein, and Colenso at the hands of skilled Boer commandos. When the British diplomat Arthur Balfour visited Windsor in deep despair, Victoria famously rebuked him: 'Please understand that there is no one depressed in this house; we are not interested in the possibilities of defeat; they do not exist!' Victoria spent her final energy visiting wounded soldiers in hospitals, knitting woolen scarves for her troops, and holding receptions for grieving military widows. Her visit to Ireland in April 1900 was a triumph of personal courage, as she rode in an open carriage through Dublin for three weeks, winning the hearts of ordinary Irish citizens.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PASSING OF THE GREAT QUEEN: OSBORNE HOUSE: JANUARY 22, 1901
In early January 1901, Queen Victoria's health failed rapidly at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight. At eighty-one, blind, frail, and drifting in and out of consciousness, her royal family gathered around her bed, including her eldest grandson, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany. On the evening of Tuesday, January 22, 1901, at six-thirty, surrounded by her weeping children, Queen Victoria died peacefully, holding the hand of the German Kaiser. She had reigned for sixty-three years, seven months, and two days—the longest reign in British history to that date. In accordance with her secret, detailed instructions, she was dressed in a white silk dress and her wedding veil, her coffin lined with mementos of Albert and John Brown. Her body was carried across the Solent on a royal yacht beneath a canopy of saluting warships, and brought to Windsor to be buried beside Prince Albert in the Royal Mausoleum at Frogmore, beneath the Latin inscription she had chosen forty years earlier: 'Vale desideratissime! Farewell, most beloved! Here at last I will rest with thee, with thee in Christ I will rise again.' The Victorian Age had reached its magnificent, immortal close. As Queen Victoria lay dying at Osborne House in January 1901, her family gathered around her bedside: her eldest son Bertie, her German grandson Kaiser Wilhelm II, and her daughters held her hands as the final moments slipped away. In accordance with her secret, detailed instructions, Albert's dressing gown, a plaster cast of his hand, and a lock of John Brown's hair were placed inside her coffin beneath an avalanche of white flowers. When her funeral train traveled from Portsmouth to London, the fleet fired minute guns across the Solent, and silent millions lined the railway tracks in solemn tribute. Victoria had reigned for sixty-three years and seven months, giving her name to an entire era of human progress, moral earnestness, and global empire.
